# Sizing a power station for a fridge

**A power station with about 1,500-2,000 Wh of capacity and a surge rating of at least 1,300 W (higher for a big or older fridge) will run a typical full-size fridge for about a day.** A ~1,000 Wh unit gets you roughly 12-17 hours.

## The three checks

1. **Surge watts:** This is the one that most often fails. The compressor spikes to about 1,000-1,800 W on startup for a standard top-freezer, and up to ~2,400 W for large or older units ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). A station with plenty of battery but a low surge rating will trip when the compressor starts ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
2. **Continuous watts:** A full-size fridge runs at about 100-250 W, which almost any 1,000 W-class station covers.
3. **Watt-hours:** The compressor only runs about a third of the time, so the average draw is far lower than the label wattage.
   - ~1,000 Wh covers most of a day, ~1,400-2,000 Wh covers a full 24 hours, and two days needs ~2,800 Wh ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator), [BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
   - Pick a **pure sine wave** inverter, which is standard on the reputable LiFePO4 models.

## Estimating your own fridge

Find the kWh/year on the yellow EnergyGuide label, then:
- Average watts = kWh/year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760
- Wh needed ≈ average watts × hours ÷ 0.85 (inverter losses) × 1.2 (headroom)

An 18 cu ft ENERGY STAR fridge (362 kWh/yr) works out to about 41 W average, or ~1,400 Wh per day. Sources vary (some assume 50-70 W average), and a big side-by-side with an ice maker can use about double ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). The DOE's Refrigerator Energy Rating Search tool can look up your model ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/how-to-size-a-portable-power-station-for-a-refrigerator-and-essential-devices/)).

## Models that fit

I couldn't open direct product pages, so these links go to the guides listing each one, where the buy links are:

- **About 1 day (~1,150-1,500 Wh):** BLUETTI AC180 (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W, 2,700 W peak, about $399-699), the top pick in [BlackBox Supplies' guide](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage). The BLUETTI AC180P (1,440 Wh, $649) is listed on [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator), but it was sold out at the maker when checked.
- **Most of a day (~1,000 Wh):** Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh, about $499, est. ~17 hours) per [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/).
- **Over a day (~2,000 Wh):** Anker SOLIX S2000 (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W, 3,000 W peak, $699.99 after coupon) on [Anker's page](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator). HomeGrid HQ also lists 2,000 Wh-class units like the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 and EcoFlow Delta 3 Max at ~33 hours for about $880-900.
- **2+ days:** You'd need ~2,800 Wh or more, such as the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 (4,096 Wh, about 2.8 days, $2,799), also on [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/).

Prices are as listed in those guides and change often, so check before buying.

## Tips
- Keep the door shut. Food is unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F with the door closed ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- Test the setup before an outage.
- If you also want to run a freezer, router, or medical device, add their watts and Wh to the totals above.

If you tell me your fridge's size or EnergyGuide kWh/year and how long an outage you want to cover, I can narrow this to one or two picks.
